resources.string: How the whole launcher looks: dark or light theme, the accent color, the photo behind Start, the style (classic, glass, droid), and the screen: rotation, how apps open, refresh rate and language. Theme files let you save the look and share it. Nothing here costs battery, except a very high refresh rate.

Your Start screen: how many tiles per row, how many Start screens, names and spacing, saved layouts, the clock and date on top, live tiles (weather, photos, messages) and how Start behaves (back to the top, lock layout, undo). Live tiles read data from your phone only when you allow it.

The Metro lock screen of the launcher: its photo, what it shows (clock, alarm, notifications, weather, next event, music), the fingerprint icon and the screensaver while charging. It does not replace your PIN or fingerprint: the security of the phone stays Android’s.

The bars around your apps. The MetroWin status bar (signal, clock, battery; it can also sit over other apps), the Action Center you pull down from the top (quick buttons, sliders, volume panel) and the navigation bar with the three Windows Phone buttons. Showing a bar over other apps needs the accessibility service, which the launcher uses only to draw it.

What your fingers can do: double tap and two-finger swipes on Start, pulls from the edges, the Recent apps tile, and how a touch feels (sound, vibration, animation speed). The voice page lets you speak to the launcher. Some gestures use the accessibility service, only to lock the screen or draw over other apps.

Your apps: what the app list shows at the top, hidden and renamed apps, icon packs and the icon of a single app, and the search box (what it looks in, what it answers, which web engine it uses). Searching in contacts, calendar or files asks for the matching permission only when you turn it on.

The mini apps built into the launcher (Messages, Mail, Calendar, Calculator, Notes and the others) have their own switches here, the same ones as in the options menu of each app. A change applies the next time the app is opened. The accent color of the mini apps is on the Look page.

How notifications reach you: the permission to read them, the banner over other apps, replies from the panel, grouping, sounds, filtering by words, timed quiet mode and choices for each app. Reading notifications needs notification access; the launcher keeps what it reads on the phone and does not send it anywhere.

What keeps your things safe: the safe mode for banking apps (the launcher takes its own windows away while one is open, because banks refuse to run under overlays), apps locked behind your fingerprint, and the kid’s corner, a Start with only the apps you choose.

How much the launcher uses the battery. Power saving makes it do less when the battery is low. Off screen, or with another app in front, the launcher runs no timers and reads nothing. Excluding it from Android’s battery optimization keeps notifications and sync alive.

Make the launcher easier to read and use: bigger or bolder text, a font of your own, fewer animations, stronger contrast, and the use of TalkBack. These apply to the whole launcher and to the mini apps. Text size is limited so that the pages never break.

Keeping your setup safe: save the layout and settings to a file or to a folder (with automatic copies), restore them, share them, sync two phones with an encrypted file in a folder you choose, and pause or hide the work profile and the private space. Nothing is sent to any server: you choose the folder.

The version of the launcher and the update from GitHub (checked only when you ask, or every 12 hours if you turn it on), information about the phone, the tutorial to see again, a bug report with the log of the app, the credits and the other projects of the author.
